\chapter{Telling Time}
\label{ch:hi-telling-time}
\hlchaptermodality{18}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can tell someone what o'clock it is in Hindi.}

Say \hi{एक} \hi{बज} \hi{रहा} \hi{है} and \hi{दो} \hi{बज} \hi{रहे} \hi{हैं} — the hour striking, exactly as the ghaṇṭā bell once did.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[ghaṇṭā / bajnā / baj rahā hai / baj …]{\hi{घंटा} / \hi{बजना} — the bell and the hours that strike}

\label{lesson:HI-C18-ghanta}



\begin{quote}
Here's a word that wears its history on its sleeve: Hindi's word for \textquotedblleft{}hour\textquotedblright{} is the exact same word as \textquotedblleft{}bell.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know — \hi{घंटा} — bell AND hour, one word}
\textbf{\hi{घंटा}} (\emph{ghanṭā}) = \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{hour}\textquotedblright{} — and it means \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{bell, gong}\textquotedblright{} just as commonly. It comes from Sanskrit \textbf{\hi{घण्टा}} (\emph{ghaṇṭā}), \textquotedblleft{}bell, gong.\textquotedblright{} The connection isn't a coincidence: temples, towns, and later clock towers historically marked the passing of time by \textbf{striking a bell} — the hour was announced by sound, not read off a face — so the word for the bell itself came to mean the unit of time it announced. Compare this to English \textbf{o'clock}, itself a worn-down \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{of the clock},\textquotedblright{} or French's \textbf{il est … heures}: different languages, but time-telling vocabulary keeps circling back to the \emph{instrument} used to mark it.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: \hi{बजना} — \textquotedblleft{}to strike, to toll\textquotedblright{}}]
Hindi tells the time with the verb \textbf{\hi{बजना}} (\emph{bajnā}), \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{to strike, to toll}\textquotedblright{} — the same imagery as a bell striking the hour:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\hi{एक} \hi{बज} \hi{रहा} \hi{है।}} — \textquotedblleft{}It is one o'clock.\textquotedblright{} (literally \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{one is striking}\textquotedblright{}) \textbf{\hi{दो} \hi{बज} \hi{रहे} \hi{हैं।}} — \textquotedblleft{}It is two o'clock.\textquotedblright{} (literally \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{two are striking}\textquotedblright{})
\end{quote}

Just like Spanish switches from singular \emph{es} to plural \emph{son} after \textquotedblleft{}one,\textquotedblright{} Hindi switches \textbf{\hi{बज} \hi{रहा} \hi{है}} (singular) to \textbf{\hi{बज} \hi{रहे} \hi{हैं}} (plural) once the count passes one — matching the number, not just tacking on \textquotedblleft{}o'clock.\textquotedblright{}
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}ghanṭā\textquotedblright{} — hour, also \textquotedblleft{}bell\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}ek baj raha hai\textquotedblright{} — it is one o'clock, \textquotedblleft{}one is striking\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}do baj rahe hain\textquotedblright{} — it is two o'clock, \textquotedblleft{}two are striking\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \textbf{\hi{घंटा}} literally mean besides \textquotedblleft{}hour\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{\textquotedblleft{}Bell, gong\textquotedblright{}} — from Sanskrit \emph{ghaṇṭā}.) Why did \textquotedblleft{}bell\textquotedblright{} come to mean \textquotedblleft{}hour\textquotedblright{}? (Because clocks/towns historically \textbf{struck a bell} to announce the hour.) What verb does Hindi use to tell the time, and what does it literally mean? (\textbf{\hi{बजना}}, \emph{bajnā} — \textquotedblleft{}to strike, to toll,\textquotedblright{} as in \emph{ek baj raha hai}, \textquotedblleft{}one is striking.\textquotedblright{})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[kha]{\hi{ख} — one character, met inside words you already say}

\label{lesson:HI-S122-letter-kha}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: \hi{ल} — what does it do?

One character this time. Just one — and you have been saying it for pages without knowing which mark on the page it was.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \hi{ख}}
\textbf{\hi{ख}} — \emph{kha}.

It is a \textbf{consonant}, and in this script a consonant is never bare: it comes with an \emph{a} already in it. So it is not \emph{kh}, it is \textbf{kha}.

You already say these, and every one of them has \hi{ख} somewhere inside it:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\hi{शिरोरेखा}} \emph{shirorekhā} — the head-line that Devanagari letters hang from
  \item \textbf{\hi{ख़ुशी}} — happiness / pleased to meet you
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Writing: \hi{ख} — copy what you see}
Put your pen on \hi{ख} and follow its line. Copy the shape you can see — slowly, and larger than it is printed.

\begin{quote}
This book does not yet tell you \textbf{where to start the character or which way to travel}. That is a real thing, taught with real variation from school to school, and it is not written down here until it can be written down with a source. Copying what is in front of you needs no such source, and it is how the shape gets into your hand in the meantime.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at these words, and find \hi{ख} in the ones that have it
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\hi{शिरोरेखा}  ·  \hi{ख़ुशी}  ·  \hi{नमस्ते}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \hi{ख} three times, saying \emph{kha} as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Look:} back at any page and find \hi{ख} once more
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which character is this — \hi{ख}? What sound does it carry? (\emph{\textbf{kha}}.) Name one word you already say that contains it.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[o]{\hi{◌ो} — a bar and a stroke}

\label{lesson:HI-S150-vowel-sign-o}



\begin{quote}
The last two marks went below the letter and above the line. Say which did which.

This one does \textbf{both sides at once}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \hi{◌ो}}
\textbf{\hi{◌ो}} — \emph{o}.

It is a \textbf{vowel sign}: it attaches to a consonant and replaces the \emph{a} built into it.

Where it sits: \textbf{the ā bar on the right, plus a stroke above the head-line}. Two pieces, one mark.

Worked through: \textbf{\hi{द}} + \textbf{\hi{◌ो}} = \textbf{\hi{दो}}.

\subsection*{Script: the second number you ever counted}
You met this mark before you could name a single letter:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\hi{दो}} — two
  \item \textbf{\hi{बोलना}} — to speak
  \item \textbf{\hi{शिरोरेखा}} — the head-line itself
\end{itemize}

\textbf{\hi{दो}} is the plainest example in the language: one consonant, one mark, one word. Look at it and the two pieces are easy to separate — the upright bar to the right of \textbf{\hi{द}}, and the short stroke riding on top.

\subsection*{Writing: \hi{◌ो} — copy what you see}
Put your pen on \textbf{\hi{◌ो}} and follow its line. Copy the shape you can see — slowly, and larger than it is printed.

\begin{quote}
This book does not yet tell you \textbf{where to start the character or which way to travel}. That is a real thing, taught with real variation from school to school, and it is not written down here until it can be written down with a source. Copying what is in front of you needs no such source, and it is how the shape gets into your hand in the meantime.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at this word and name its two pieces
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\hi{दो}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \hi{दो} three times, saying \emph{do} as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Say it:} which side of the letter each piece of the mark sits on
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What two pieces make \textbf{\hi{◌ो}}? (A bar on the right and a stroke above.) What vowel does it put on its consonant? Name the number you count that is one consonant and this mark.
\end{tcolorbox}
